title: We Tested One of the Best Athletes on the PGA TOUR | Michael Brennan’s TPI Assessment

people.team: Longstanding swing coach, trainer and caddy contribute; preserve roles without relying on uncertain automatic-caption spellings.
people.attribution_basis: Source title, named dialogue and on-camera demonstrations

context.level: Tour player with high existing speed and established team
context.body_context: Formal in-person screen is shown. No numerical body-handicap score provided. Clinical remarks remain source context, not app diagnoses.
context.style: Detailed measurement-led assessment followed by simple task-specific instructions, contrasts and teach-back

coverage.transcript_kind: Full YouTube en-orig automatic caption text, 204 reading-index blocks
coverage.visual_review_method: 102 full-timeline overview frames, 172 targeted detail frames, 36 graph-context frames and 36 rehearsal/contrast frames. All 30 contact sheets inspected. Some timestamps repeat; sampled inspection, not continuous playback.
limitations: 480p video; filmed monitors have glare and small text. Clear full-screen graph inserts separately identified.
Edited outdoor, lab and interview inserts are not a chronological trial log.
Automatic captions include ambiguous technical words and inconsistent short summaries.
No raw 3D/force/launch export or controlled before/after dataset.

evidence.attribution: Greg Rose and Dave Phillips, with Michael Brennan and his team
evidence.summary: Interview distinguishes the reported fault from the actual problem: Brennan thinks hanging back causes an excessively left path and dislikes the high finish. Rose asks whether he would mind hanging back if path were acceptable. Long clubs favour a fade; shorter irons are described as straighter. These are the initial hypotheses, not confirmed findings.

frames.observation: Brennan describes his driver-path concern.

limitations: Source interpretation, not independently validated biomechanics.

evidence.summary: Physical screen includes pelvic tilting and segment separation, squat variations, foot alignment, ankle testing and hip comparison. Right side feels tighter/pinchy in some positions. Rose investigates manually and does not recommend replacing the existing programme.

evidence.attribution: Greg Rose and Dave Phillips, with Michael Brennan and his team
evidence.summary: Rose checks trunk asymmetry, leg motion, balance, shoulder/neck movement, loaded hip rotation and seated trunk rotation. He distinguishes adequate unloaded range from reduced loaded right-hip rotation as a possible stability/guarding issue. Left trunk rotation is reported around 43 degrees versus 61 right, new to the trainer. Findings suggest possibilities to compare with the swing, not proof of causation.

evidence.attribution: Greg Rose and Dave Phillips, with Michael Brennan and his team
evidence.summary: Existing trainer records indicate high strength. Power tests report roughly 26-inch jump, 24-foot sit-up throw, 23-foot chest pass and grip readings 72/66 with units not clear in captions. evidence.summary: Driver force review is praised for lateral-rock-twist-jump peak sequence and unusually early force timing relative to shaft position. The graphic explicitly labelled Driver: Full Kinetic Sequence shows peak order 1/2/3/4 and max row 19/26/20/188. A skeleton accompanies the timing discussion.

evidence.attribution: Greg Rose and Dave Phillips, with Michael Brennan and his team
evidence.summary: 3D discussion reports about 125 degrees thorax turn and roughly 21-25 degrees extension. The initially suspected arch is accepted in the context of this large turn and strong overall swing. A core-engagement brake is optional if the team wants less length or greater control, not a mandatory repair.

evidence.attribution: Greg Rose and Dave Phillips, with Michael Brennan and his team
evidence.summary: Iron kinetics are later than driver. TPI describes lateral force peaking before the top with driver but after the start down with iron, and iron pelvis setup farther back relative to stance than expected. They connect this to the reported hanging-back issue. Spoken lateral push is about 19 percent body weight driver versus 23 iron.

Multiple 3D traces visible during pelvis/trunk review.

limitations: The clear driver table verifies 19, but iron 23 and the precise iron peak timing are retained as spoken readings.
No precise millisecond difference or matched raw trials available.

evidence.attribution: Greg Rose and Dave Phillips, with Michael Brennan and his team
evidence.summary: Further force review mentions driver lead-side braking lower than trail push despite the broadly favourable driver assessment. Simulated bunker kinematics are more full-swing-like than desired. Table reports trunk 573 and lead-arm 746, with other velocities. Pelvis backswing sway is read as 2.2 inches and trunk 1.4 inches. TPI links the unstable base to variable sand entry, and proposes avoiding backward pelvis travel.

frames.observation: Skeleton at the iron timing reference.

Separate trunk-position graph appears while 1.4-inch motion is discussed.

limitations: Source mechanical explanation is preserved as TPI reasoning, not independently verified causality.
Negative on the target axis means away from target. Do not confuse position, force and angular velocity.
Driver braking caveat does not become a prescribed driver overhaul.

evidence.summary: Final proposal is simple and club-specific: iron pelvis more centred or slightly forward relative to stance, keep it there in backswing, then go. Preserve the driver. The goal is earlier useful action without a large deliberate chest shift.

cases.title: Define the performance problem and preserve a good-day baseline
cases.coaching_finding: Analytical elite player suspects a fault and dislikes some appearances; caddy reports frustration after isolated imperfect shots.
cases.coach_reasoning: Ask what observable outcome is wrong, then compare with known good data and the established team's history. A disliked appearance alone need not require correction.

intervention.process: Separate golfer report, coach hypothesis and measured evidence. Record club, intended flight and actual miss.
intervention.attention: Give the player a small set of useful checks and one current intention.
intervention.baseline: Retain good-day captures for future comparison.

applicability: Player reports a fault, perceived aesthetic problem or sudden loss of confidence.
Known shot intent and meaningful performance outcome.
unknowns: No mental-health diagnosis or tested psychological intervention.
One poor shot does not establish a durable pattern.
cases.observed_result: Assessment narrows attention to iron setup, bunker base and putting perception while largely preserving driver. No later scoring results.

selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Check whether the suspected fault co-occurs with the actual miss and differs from a good baseline.

cases.title: Use loaded and unloaded screening as context for swing hypotheses
cases.coaching_finding: Source finds mild right-side restrictions/control differences and asymmetric trunk rotation, with otherwise strong screening performance.
cases.coach_reasoning: Rose contrasts manually available range with reduced loaded range and considers guarding/stability. He explicitly needs the swing to show a matching effect before making a body-swing connection.

intervention.process: Preserve screen result, test position, assessor interpretation and uncertainty separately.
intervention.training: Existing trainer handles pelvic control and relevant physical work; no new detailed exercise prescription given.

applicability: A real physical assessment is available with test context.
A separately observed swing pattern may be related, without assuming causation.
unknowns: No diagnosis of tissue pathology, scoliosis, pain source or a body handicap score.
Current app video cannot substitute for manual screening or force/mobility measurements.
cases.observed_result: Physical context informs later investigation; final intervention remains modest. No physical retest after training.

selection.coaching_focus: Use assessed body context when available
selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Verify the proposed connection against actual swing/task data; leave cause unknown when assessment is absent.

cases.title: High capacity can rule out general power as the first coaching priority
cases.coaching_finding: Brennan already has high strength/power results and reports approximately 126 mph cruising driver speed.
cases.coach_reasoning: TPI distinguishes capacity from technique/equipment efficiency; insufficient general power is not the obvious bottleneck in this case.

intervention.decision: Prioritise the identified control/timing problems rather than automatically prescribing more strength or speed work.

applicability: Reliable capacity tests and swing outcomes in the same golfer.
unknowns: Test protocols and some units incomplete.
Source tour-average statements are inconsistent and not a normative dataset.
cases.observed_result: Coaching proceeds to task-specific setup and timing; no speed-gain programme tested.

selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Use comparable individual testing and performance; do not infer jump or grip capacity from a swing video.

cases.title: Preserve an efficient driver despite unconventional-looking details
cases.coaching_finding: Player worries about foot banking, high finish and long/arched-looking backswing. Driver data is broadly favourable.
cases.coach_reasoning: 3D/force review places visible features in context. Large thorax turn accompanies extension; an unattractive foot position alone is not proof of hanging back.

intervention.decision: Keep the normal driver pattern. Optional length-control experiment is a separate case.
intervention.qualification: Retain the later lead-side braking observation as a caveat, not evidence that all driver metrics were perfect.

applicability: Driver performance and reliable assessment support efficiency.
No demonstrated need for a specific change solely to match another player's appearance.
unknowns: Source biomechanical/safety explanations are not independently validated.
No universal turn/extension ratio or ideal heel pattern.
cases.observed_result: Driver retained as default; optional core trial later. No claim that one lab assessment proves lifetime safety.

selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Reconsider only with a relevant outcome, new data or a specific shot-control need.

cases.title: Optional core engagement creates a felt endpoint for a long backswing
cases.coaching_finding: Trying to shorten arms feels weak because Brennan does not feel a natural end to his turn.
cases.coach_reasoning: TPI proposes controlling extra extension to create resistance while retaining coil. This is optional; existing long-driver timing may suit him.

intervention.feel: Keep the chest/abdomen connection plugged in through the turn.
intervention.demonstration: Compare turning with an arched versus more controlled pelvic position to feel the endpoint.
intervention.practice: Train pelvic control with his trainer; do not consciously reproduce the pelvic-tilt screen during full swings.
intervention.use: An optional control shot or response to unwanted length, not an obligatory default.

applicability: Player wants a shorter swing and needs a felt endpoint.
Evidence of extra turn/extension relevant to length, with a suitable physical context.
unknowns: No universal spine angle or prescribed bracing force.
No matched speed/accuracy trial; 10-15-degree reduction is a coach estimate.
cases.observed_result: Player reports resistance and likes the feel; later attempts praised after initially imperfect contact. Coaches still say it is not needed all the time.

selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Compare contact, useful speed, dispersion and comfort; retain ordinary driver if no benefit.

cases.title: Iron hang-back case: pelvis setup and earlier force, not extra chest travel
cases.coaching_finding: Iron assessment shows later force timing and pelvis position/motion farther back than desired. Existing get-left cue includes chest movement and extra travel before pushing.
cases.coach_reasoning: Starting the pelvis appropriately relative to stance and preventing early backward drift can reduce the travel needed before useful force. Long-iron ball position must be reconsidered after this change.

intervention.primary: Set pelvis centre near stance centre or modestly ahead according to the iron; retain that position through early backswing.
intervention.feel: Resist the pelvis being pushed away in P1-P2. Let chest turn; leave efficient downswing alone.
intervention.progression: Eight iron first, then longer irons. Move ball modestly forward if the new body relation makes it effectively too far back.
intervention.reference: Plumb bob means centre of pelvis relative to centre of stance, not the ball and not pressure percentage.

applicability: Iron-specific backward pelvis setup/drift supported by suitable view or measurement.
Timing claims require force-plate evidence; visual displacement alone is insufficient.
Actual contact/path problem and shot intent.
unknowns: No matched post-change force/path/dispersion export.
Setup wording shifts through the source; use the explicit final stance-centre clarification, preserving the ambiguity log.
Inch values are source examples, not body-size-independent thresholds.
cases.observed_result: Player reports different loading; face-on video is said to show reduced drift, contact is praised and divots appear more right. These are qualitative retests.

selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Check actual pelvis motion, contact and start/curve; use force data if claiming timing improved. Add ball adjustment only if needed.

cases.title: Putting line looks wrong: test ball position before changing the stroke
cases.coaching_finding: Known ball-line aim appears left from address to this right-handed player; source labels him same-side eye dominant.
cases.coach_reasoning: Use a fixed independently checked line and change one setup variable. Here ball fore/aft affects perception more than open/closed stance, despite general eye-dominance tendencies discussed.

intervention.test: Set a verified ball line, address without re-aiming, report where it looks aimed, then test fore/aft ball position and stance changes.
intervention.selection: Move ball modestly forward from this player's habit to the location where perception matches.
intervention.practice: Repeat with right/left break and uphill/downhill conditions; retain speed and start-line checks.

applicability: A reproducible mismatch between checked aim and perceived aim.
Player feedback is available; eye dominance or confidence cannot be read from video alone.
unknowns: No prescription solely from eye dominance.
No quantified putting improvement, vision diagnosis or ideal universal ball position.
cases.observed_result: Player says the slightly forward location looks better aligned. Open/closed exaggerations were less helpful.

selection.coaching_focus: One ball-position experiment around a checked line
selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Confirm perception across putts, then start line and speed; avoid assuming confidence proves a correct read.

cases.title: Bunker entry control through pelvis stability and a balanced starting feel
cases.coaching_finding: Simulated bunker data shows 2.2-inch backward pelvic travel. Real bunker trials connect drifting back with heavy entry and poor high-soft control.
cases.coach_reasoning: Backward pelvic travel shifts the bottom of the swing. Excessive left lean can also encourage falling back, so the later instruction uses a roughly balanced starting feel and then motion towards the target.

intervention.primary: Avoid the initial pelvis move away from target while pivoting.
intervention.rehearsal: Use the demonstrated resisted early-backswing rehearsal to feel the difference.
intervention.starting_feel: Roughly balanced rather than all-left. Keep pelvis distinct from chest.
intervention.contrast: Deliberately drift once in the teaching comparison to identify the old feel, then return to the intended pattern.

applicability: Bunker task with evidence of pelvic drift and inconsistent sand entry.
Sand/lie and equipment considered; do not import full-swing power sequence as ideal.
unknowns: Position is not pressure. 50/50 and related ratios were not read from outdoor force plates.
Exact sand-entry distance and improvement are not independently measured.
cases.observed_result: Deliberately wrong drift attempt called heavy; later shots praised with different sound and player recognition of the changed feel.

selection.policy_origin: User preference for one focus and at most two compatible cues. Source assessment contains multiple tasks, alternatives and a longer recap.
selection.reassess: Check repeatable entry and useful flight; if excessively left setup prompts falling back, reduce the initial lean.

cases.title: High soft bunker shot: lower handle and more room after the base is stable
cases.coaching_finding: Bunker setup appears square/tall and too much like pitch/full-swing delivery for the requested high soft shot.
cases.coach_reasoning: Phillips seeks lower handle and more room to let the open club work under the ball; TPI also notes the source bunker kinematic pattern differs from that of their preferred finesse examples.
